author: distortgeekin
content:
Harness engineering keeps one agent honest. Graph engineering is what decides whether ten of them are worth the tokens.

Right now the timeline is full of one specific screenshot. An agent that "tracks" ten others. Ships code while its owner sleeps. Calls itself something like a Chief of Staff.

Almost none of these posts explain how the tracking actually works. What decides which of the ten agents runs next. What happens when two of them disagree. When the whole thing is supposed to stop.

That missing piece has a name. It is the graph.

A harness keeps one agent honest. It stops that one agent from lying to you about work it did not do, or shipping a fix that only looks like a fix. That is a real layer and it is worth building.

A graph is a different layer entirely. It decides which agent runs, in what order, based on what has already happened - not on what you guessed at design time. Skip it and what you actually built is a chain: a fixed script that calls Agent A, then Agent B, then Agent C, no matter what any of them find along the way.

Anthropic's own engineering team has watched this exact failure in production. Teams built a separate agent for planning, execution, review and iteration, and lost context at every handoff - ending up spending more tokens coordinating than actually working.

The 30-second version:

> Harness = keeps one agent honest
Loop = lets it get better run over run
Graph = decides which agent runs next, and when to stop

## Part 1: A Chain Is Not A Graph

1. A chain has no state that survives a handoff.

Each step in a hardcoded pipeline starts blind to what the last one actually found - only what got summarized into its prompt by whoever wired the pipeline together. That is exactly the failure Anthropic named: multi-agent setups that spend more time coordinating than working, because nothing in the system genuinely shares what has already been learned. The context does not travel. It gets re-typed, badly, at every hop.

2. A chain cannot route around what it did not predict.

Graph-based frameworks like LangGraph model this as nodes, edges and state: nodes do the work, edges decide what runs next, and a shared state object is what every edge actually reads to make that decision. A conditional edge fires because the state now says something that makes it the right move - not because a branch was written in advance for exactly this case. A chain has no such thing. It runs A, then B, then C, whether B found anything worth acting on or not.

3. A chain does not know when to stop.

Without a state field that says the work is done, a chain runs every step to the end regardless of whether step one already answered the question. That is exactly where the token bill balloons for zero extra output - the system keeps working because nothing told it not to, not because there is anything left worth doing.

![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSGPl7wW4A41oIh.png)

> chain: Agent A -> Agent B -> Agent C, always, no matter what
graph: Agent A -> [state says what to do next] -> Agent B or Agent D or stop

## Part 2: What A Real Graph Buys You

4. Parallel fan-out without losing the plan.

Anthropic's own Research system is the real version of this. A lead agent plans the work, spins up three to five subagents in parallel, and a single synthesis pass turns their separate findings into one answer with its own citation step. On Anthropic's internal evaluation, that setup beat a single well-prompted agent by 90.2 percent - at roughly fifteen times the token cost of one normal chat turn, and it cut total research time by up to 90 percent on the complex, genuinely parallelizable queries it was built for. The graph is the specific thing that let five independent workers run at once without their results colliding into each other.

![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSGPrbeWcAImh_g.png)

5. Conditional routing based on what actually happened.

In that same model, an edge does not fire because someone wrote it into a script ahead of time. It fires because the shared state now contains something that makes it the correct next move. That is what lets a system revisit a step, retry with new information, or skip a stage entirely - all things a fixed pipeline will happily run anyway, because a fixed pipeline cannot see what just happened.

6. State that survives the whole run, not just one hop.

Every node in a real graph reads the same shared object and writes back into it. An agent three steps downstream can act directly on something the very first agent found, without a human - or a worse agent - summarizing it into a prompt by hand somewhere in the middle.

## Part 3: Where Most Teams Get It Wrong

7. Building the graph before checking if you need one.

Anthropic names three specific situations where multiple agents actually beat one: when context genuinely pollutes a single agent's window, when the sub-tasks are truly parallelizable, and when different specializations improve which tools get picked. Outside those three, the coordination cost typically outruns the benefit - and Anthropic has watched teams spend months building an elaborate multi-agent architecture, only to find a better-prompted single agent matched the result.

8. Confusing more agents with more graph.

A "Chief of Staff" agent watching five copies of the same worker is a dashboard, not a graph - unless the thing watching it actually changes what happens next based on what it sees. If the routing never changes no matter what the workers report back, giving the orchestrator a name does not add a layer. It adds a screenshot.

![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSGPwZFaMAA2oQQ.png)

9. Never pricing the coordination against the baseline.

Multi-agent systems typically run three to ten times the tokens of an equivalent single-agent pass, by Anthropic's own measurement, once you count duplicated context, coordination messages between agents, and the summarizing that happens at every handoff. None of the viral screenshots this week mention that number. It is the one that actually decides whether the setup is worth running at all.

## The Mistakes

The naive chain. Hardcoding the step order in your own code instead of letting shared state decide it. Fix: make the next step a function of state, not a line number in a script you wrote before seeing any real output.

The context cliff. Every agent starts blind to what the last one actually found. Fix: pass the object the graph maintains, not a paraphrase someone typed by hand between steps.

Counting agents instead of edges. "Twenty agents running" describes headcount, not architecture. Fix: count the conditional edges instead - the decisions the system is actually making on its own, without you.

Skipping the token audit. Shipping a multi-agent system that was never compared against one well-prompted agent doing the same job. Fix: run the single-agent baseline first, every time, and only add a second agent once it demonstrably loses.

The loop with no exit. Agents that keep re-triggering each other because nothing in the shared state ever says the work is done. Fix: an explicit stop condition written into the state, not a timeout you are hoping is generous enough.

## Conclusion

A harness keeps one agent from lying to you about its own work. A graph decides which agent runs next, and when the whole thing is actually finished.

Most of what is going viral this week has plenty of the first layer and almost none of the second - a stack of agents, and a name for whoever is supposedly watching them, with no real routing underneath any of it.

Before you add a second agent to anything, write down the one condition that would change what your system does next. If you cannot name it, you do not have a graph yet. You have two copies of the same prompt and a dashboard that watches them both do the same thing.

P.S. The cheapest version of this to try today is not a new agent. It is one field in your existing state that the next step actually reads before it decides what to do. That single field, read by the next step, is graph engineering at its smallest possible size.

Bookmark this before it gets buried.
title: Everyone Is Building Agent Teams. Nobody Is Building The Graph
